pr_title: promql(histograms): Change sample total calculation for histograms
pr_body:
- This PR changes the way of number samples are calculated when doing query operations with
histograms.

- Added method for `FloatHistogram`s that calculates the size in bytes of the whole struct
and its fields.

- Added method that calculates number of samples (4 bytes per sample) of histogram in
`HPoint` struct.

Fixes #11555
pr_comments: I believe https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/d6e1b1acdb1231f5bb694bc482b568ccea2b40af/promql/engine.go#L1238 and https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/d6e1b1acdb1231f5bb694bc482b568ccea2b40af/promql/engine.go#L1241 need an update, too. Which means we have to dive into the `Vector` and check if it is a float sample or a histogram sample.

issue_context.title: promql (histograms): Reevaluate weight of native histograms relevant for `--query.max-samples`
issue_context.body:
### Proposal

Currently, each native histogram counts as one sample against the limit given by `--query.max-samples`. However, a histogram has a count, a sum, and an arbitrary number of buckets. We could move to the opposite end of the spectrum and count each of those as one sample. But maybe it makes sense to do something in between. This requires an evaluation of the memory impact of native histograms vs. conventional simple float samples.
comments:
Summary of thoughts from the sync meeting:

- Currently, a sample in memory will be 8 bytes for the float and 8 bytes for the timestamp.
- A histogram will have 8 byte for the timestamp and then have 8 byte value for the count, the sum, and for each bucket.
- So maybe the base weight of a histogram with 0 buckets should be 1.5, and then add 0.5 per bucket.
- We can add additional detail: `promql.HPoint` has a pointer to a histogram, while `promql.FPoint` contains the float value directly. So that would add another 8 bytes. Then the `FloatHistogram` structure has a bunch of fields.
- Which would lead to a much higher base weight per histogram (depending on the in-memory size of a `FloatHistogram` struct), and then still plus 0.5 per bucket.
@marctc plans to work on this next week.

review_comments: The doc comment here should be updated to reflect that histograms are taken into account in a weighted fashion.
I think we need + 16 here because we also have to take into account the pointer to the `FloatHistogram` (8 bytes).
but `Size()` already has the size of pointer, right?

if `H` is a pointer, it would return the size of a pointer (8 bytes on a 64bit architecture).
if `H` is not a pointer, it returns the size of the actual thing, but not including the size a pointer would have if it pointed to the thing.

For a float sample, we store the float64 directly, but for histogram samples, we store a pointer to the histogram _plus_ the histogram itself.

Sorry, now I get it, you mean you designed the `Size` method such that it already includes the pointer size.

Then it makes sense.

I'm pretty sure we cannot have this in the hot path. It's way too expensive. Also, we should avoid the `unsafe` package wherever we can.

This is great to learn about the size, but once we know it, we should hardcode all the numbers currently retrieved via `unsafe.Sizeof`. This can be a bit tricky because some of them might depend on the architecture. If you find a clever way to take that into account, great. But we can also assume 64bit architectures for the purpose of this safeguard. (Prometheus on 32bit isn't really viable for larger payloads anyway.
> I'm pretty sure we cannot have this in the hot path.

Do you mean as method of the `FloatHistogram` struct? Why not? Where would you put it instead?

> It's way too expensive. 

Expensive in terms of computation? Is it really?

> Also, we should avoid the `unsafe` package wherever we can.

Why? It's been used in other parts of the codebase

> > I'm pretty sure we cannot have this in the hot path.
> 
> Do you mean as method of the `FloatHistogram` struct? Why not? Where would you put it instead?

I guess it's fine to have a "size" method, but we cannot calculate the size from first principles each time. Most of it is static and only depends on the architecture. The dynamic parts (i.e. `len` of slices) is OK to calculate dynamically each time. (At least we can try and see if it has an unacceptable impact on performance.)

> > It's way too expensive. 
>
> Expensive in terms of computation? Is it really?

This is just housekeeping. It shouldn't take more than a few percent of total compute time. Plus, it's easy to avoid all the "static" parts. As said above, just the various `len` of slices need to be calculated dynamically. And that's (maybe and hopefully) cheap enaugh.

> > Also, we should avoid the `unsafe` package wherever we can.
>
> Why? It's been used in other parts of the codebase

And it's _very_ frowned upon. (Anecdote: At Gophercon, one of the semi-famous Gophers there asked my what I'm working on. I said: "Prometheus". They said: "I feel sorry for you." I: "Why?" They: "Isn't it using the `unsafe` package?") Obviously, we shouldn't let anecdotes drive our development, but any use of `unsafe` needs an _exceptionally_ strong justification because it breaks the safety guarantees of Go. Even the current uses are often doubted (also within the Prometheus community, not only by outsiders). And this use here is very easy to avoid, see above.

So I would suggest to pre-calculate all the "static" parts (how large is the baseline usage of a slice, how large is a float64, etc.) and just put the constant values in the actual code (with a comment how you calculated it), and then add the dynamic parts (e.g. `len(fh.PositiveSpans) * 8`, assuming a `Span` takes 8 bytes) in a dynamic fashion. You can just do it for 64bit architectures for now and add a TODO to add refined calculation for 32bit architectures later (or do it right now if you like, you can use suffixes in the file name or build tags to decide which code is used for which architecture).
